newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX gasoline ends up as greater demand expected.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX gasoline ends up as greater demand expected.

text.p: NYMEX gasoline rose Wednesday in early anticipation of its seasonal spring rally before the summer driving season.
"You have some guys getting into gasoline early because while people are looking for this market to bottom, they also don't want to miss the rally," said Prudential Securities trader Mike DeLuca.
March gasoline ended up 0.52 cent a gallon at 64.68 cents. Oil prices have suffered recently due to poor refined product demand, with seasonally mild weather resulting in little need for heating oil.

Dealers have been selling heating oil to buy gasoline which typically experiences its greatest demand during the summer. In fact, dealers said gasoline demand has probably bottomed after hitting a two-year low two weeks ago.
The gasoline-to-heating oil spread rose to 5.09 cents from 4.74 cents Thursday and 3.44 cents last Friday.

March heating oil ended up 0.17 cent a gallon at 59.59 cents while March crude finished up 27 cents a barrel at $22.79. Dealers attributed crude's rise to short covering in the prompt month ahead of the expiry of the March contract on Thursday.
March crude was able to break resistance of $22.75 late session after testing it several times Tuesday and Wednesday.
But, dealers said crude prices may give up their gains Thursday due weekly oil inventory data from the American Petroleum Institute (API) which was reported Wednesday after the market's close.
"The API's should certainly be on the bearish side (for crude)," said a dealer, noting a healthy build in crude stocks. The data reflects the week ended February 14.
The API reported crude stocks grew a healthy 3.12 million barrels, in line with expectations, while gasoline stocks showed a surprising decline.

The API said gasoline stocks dropped 1.27 million barrels when traders had been expecting a build of about one million barrels. Distillate stocks, which reflect heating oil and diesel, fell 2.90 million barrels, in line with expectations.
Meanwhile, the market failed to react to news that China's top leader Deng Xiaoping died Wednesday at the age of 93.

China's official Xinhua news agency said Xiaoping died of complications from Parkinson's disease and a lung infection. China is a key part of Asia's growing demand for oil, analysts said. Still, analysts said Xiaoping death's meant little change in China's politics in the near term, so oil prices instead reflected domestic fundamentals Wednesday.
-- Harry Milling, New York Energy Desk, 212-859-1761
